# IELTS Writing Task 2 one-hour course — transcript synthesis

**Source:** IELTS Advantage, [Prepare for IELTS Writing in 1 Hour: Step-by-Step Course](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA), video ID h2uF03zKaCA. YouTube’s auto-generated English transcript was exported and reviewed through the end. This is the shorter, guided essay-writing course in the supplied playlist; it overlaps with the six-hour Task 2 course but has its own practice sequence and examples.

The video works through one double-question essay about robots performing more work at home and work. It pauses for workbook tasks at each stage and closes with a complete sample essay.

## 1. Classify the question and preserve every required part

The teacher uses five common Task 2 prompt families: opinion, discussion, causes/solutions, advantages/disadvantages, and double questions. This is a useful teaching taxonomy; prompts can combine requirements, so always follow the exact wording rather than relying on a label. The example prompt asks both why robot use is increasing and whether the trend is positive or negative. A response that answers only the cause question but gives no position is incomplete. ([0:36–4:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=36s))

The course’s first diagnostic framework is to read three layers:

1. **General topic:** for example, technology.
2. **Specific focus:** robots replacing or taking on human tasks at home and at work.
3. **Instruction words:** explain why this is happening and evaluate the development as positive or negative.

The purpose is to stop the learner from writing everything they know about a broad topic and to keep every paragraph tied to the actual question. ([6:45–9:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=405s))

## 2. Choose a position and produce workable ideas

For prompts that request a position, choose the side that is easiest to support clearly. The instructor says it need not be the learner’s deepest personal conviction; either side can work if the answer is relevant and developed. This is a practical exam-planning option, not an instruction to misrepresent personal beliefs. ([9:58–11:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=598s))

The teacher criticizes open-ended brainstorming because it can generate many vague or irrelevant ideas, consume time, and leave the learner with too many options. He offers a “direct method”: ask the question directly, choose a simple relevant response that can be explained, and move on. Other versions are to select the simplest workable idea or consider the answer many people might give. The review checks are whether the idea is understandable, directly relevant, and possible for the learner to develop. ([11:49–20:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=709s))

For the robot prompt, the course develops two manageable ideas: technological progress has made robots more capable; the trend can reduce people’s routine workload. The lesson is depth over a list: an ordinary idea that can be explained and supported is more useful than an impressive idea the writer cannot develop. The teacher says there are no extra marks simply for choosing complex ideas. ([14:51–20:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=891s))

## 3. Plan before drafting

The teacher describes planning as a way to prevent getting lost during writing. A short outline can identify each question, the chosen position, and the main idea that will answer it. In this double-question example, the introduction also provides a compact plan for the body paragraphs. The learner does not need a full draft in the planning space. ([20:19–22:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=1219s))

This supports the broader course practice loop: analyze the prompt, decide the answer, select relevant ideas, plan their order, then draft. The “one or two minutes” and introduction-as-plan advice are the instructor’s workflow and should be adjusted to the learner’s actual timing and writing process.

## 4. Write an introduction that is clear and answer-focused

For this double-question example, the instructor’s introduction has three functions:

1. Paraphrase the prompt accurately.
2. Briefly answer the first question.
3. Briefly state the position on the second question.

He says the introduction can be short and that there is no universal word or sentence count. It should help the reader predict the response. A classroom “stranger test” asks whether someone given only the prompt and introduction could tell what the writer thinks and what the essay will address. ([22:27–25:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=1347s), [33:30–35:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=2010s))

The paraphrase method combines close synonyms, changing word forms where appropriate, and restructuring the sentence. Check that it preserves the original meaning, is grammatical, and changes enough language naturally. Do not replace a word with a loose synonym just to avoid repetition; if a precise substitute is unavailable, keeping the original word can be better than changing the meaning. The lesson warns against forcing words such as “plethora” or ornate phrases that the learner does not control. ([24:50–32:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=1490s))

Avoid memorized hooks, proverbs, and generic background openings that do not help answer the question. The useful principle is clarity and relevance. The instructor’s claim that an examiner will literally ignore or “delete” such language is his rhetorical phrasing, not an official marking rule. ([22:32–24:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=1352s))

## 5. Build each body paragraph from one developed idea

The instructor’s scaffold for a body paragraph is:

1. **Topic sentence:** state one relevant point that answers the task.
2. **Explanation:** show what the point means and why it supports the answer.
3. **Example:** make the reasoning concrete with evidence or a plausible illustration.

A useful test for the topic sentence is whether it acts like a signpost: can the reader immediately tell what this paragraph will explain? It should connect to the ideas promised in the introduction. General statements about the topic are not enough if they fail to state the paragraph’s specific point. ([35:21–50:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=2121s))

The “shopping list” error is a paragraph that moves through four or five new claims without developing any of them. Instead, choose one or two points and explain them fully. To develop an explanation, ask “So what?” or imagine explaining the idea to a reader who knows little about the topic. These prompts help reveal missing links in the reasoning. Keep the paragraph explanatory rather than adding loosely related facts. ([38:34–57:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=2314s))

An example should support the exact topic sentence and explanation. It may be a real-world example, an everyday example, or a plausible illustration. A personal anecdote alone may not support a general claim; connect it to the point being made. The instructor warns against inventing precise statistics or attributing numbers to named studies without a sound basis. The course also advises against treating one individual experience as proof of a general trend. ([57:25–1:05:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=3445s))

The teacher’s illustrative robot essay narrows from an AI-related cause, to how data and learning allow machines to perform tasks, to a specific example of machines learning from data. For the positive view, it explains how automation can reduce routine work and uses a plausible domestic-robot example. The teaching point is the logical connection from claim to explanation to support, not the essay’s claims about any company’s current technology. ([1:05:52–1:11:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=3952s))

## 6. Keep the essay coherent from start to finish

Coherence is presented as making the argument easy to follow; cohesion is the way ideas and parts of the response connect. Keep the same position and main ideas consistent in the introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion. Do not promise one reason in the introduction, develop a different reason in the body, and introduce new ideas at the end. The essay’s organization should make the progression visible without relying on a pile of linking words. ([45:56–50:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=2756s))

The instructor calls the introduction a promise and the body the fulfillment of it. For this worked prompt, the conclusion restates the position and summarizes the same two answers in fresh wording. A clear position should remain consistent throughout the response. ([1:11:38–1:18:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=4298s))

## 7. Conclude and proofread

The course’s conclusion has three parts: a simple closing transition such as “In conclusion,” a restatement of the position, and a brief summary of the main ideas. The conclusion should not become vague or reverse the opinion. The sample feedback emphasizes that repeating the central answer in new wording is clearer than inventing a new thought to avoid any repeated vocabulary. ([1:11:38–1:18:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=4298s))

For proofreading, the instructor recommends checking at three levels: after each sentence, after each paragraph, and once across the whole essay. Check sentence-level grammar, spelling, and word choice; paragraph-level logic and development; then whole-essay structure and consistency. He also recommends identifying recurring errors through practice essays so they can be repaired before test day. This is a detailed coaching routine, not an official requirement to reread every sentence exactly three times. ([1:18:25–1:23:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=4705s))

The video argues for reserving about five minutes for review, but says time control comes from writing more efficiently through practice rather than relying on generic time tricks. Treat five minutes as an instructor target. Use timed practice and the current official task timing to set a realistic plan. The video includes a complete sample double-question essay at the end; the sample is a model to analyze, not language to copy. ([1:18:25–1:24:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h2uF03zKaCA&t=4705s))

## Official-criteria and source caveats

The instructor explains his method through Task Response, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy. The fixed assessment details should be taken from the official criteria linked in the [course blueprint](../course-blueprint.md), not from this transcript alone. The teacher’s class anecdotes, paid-course claims, sample-student bands, and promises about likely score gains are not independently verified here. His assertion that IELTS partners recently prohibited the use of invented examples or statistics should also be checked before it is presented as an official policy. The safer writing principle is to use relevant, coherent, credible support and avoid fabricated numerical evidence.

## Course-design takeaways

- Make learners mark the general topic, specific focus, and every instruction before planning.
- Use prompt-specific answer plans; teach double questions as two obligations that must both be answered.
- Teach paraphrase as accurate restatement, not synonym substitution for its own sake.
- Prioritize ideas learners can explain and support over abstract, impressive-sounding ideas.
- Model one point per paragraph and move from claim to explanation to example.
- Have learners check whether examples actually prove the paragraph’s point and whether their position stays consistent throughout.
- Use the stranger test for introductions and a structured self-review checklist after essays.
- Keep the teacher’s two-body-paragraph structure, sample time target, and other workflow choices clearly labelled as scaffolds, not official rules.
